title: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia
subject: Pathology
summary: ALL is a rapid proliferation of immature lymphoid precursors in bone marrow and blood. Diagnosis relies on morphology, immunophenotype and cytogenetics. Prompt recognition and risk‑adapted therapy improve survival, even in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is a clonal expansion of lymphoblasts that replaces normal haematopoiesis. Diagnosis requires ≥20 % lymphoblasts on peripheral smear or marrow, TdT positivity and lineage‑specific markers (CD19, CD10, CD34).
b: ≥20 % lymphoblasts on bone‑marrow aspirate
TdT⁺ confirms lymphoid origin
Immunophenotype distinguishes B‑ALL (CD19, CD10) from T‑ALL (cCD3, CD7)

t.b: Does the patient have circulating blasts? → Presence of blasts suggests leukaemia; absence does not exclude marrow disease.
What is the blast percentage? → ≥20 % confirms acute leukaemia; lower percentages require repeat or flow cytometry.
Which lineage markers are present? → CD19/CD10 = B‑ALL; cCD3/CD7 = T‑ALL; guides therapy.
Are favourable or high‑risk chromosomal abnormalities present? → t(12;21) favourable; Ph‑like or KMT2A rearrangement high‑risk.

sections.p: Risk stratification combines age, white‑cell count, cytogenetics and early treatment response (MRD). This determines intensity of chemotherapy.
b: Age < 1 yr or > 10 yr = higher risk
WBC > 50 × 10⁹/L at presentation = higher risk
MRD > 0.01 % after induction = high risk

sections.p: Most cases are de novo, but several exposures increase risk, especially in East Africa.
b: Prior exposure to ionising radiation
Chronic infection with HIV or EBV
Inherited syndromes (Down, Fanconi anaemia)
Environmental pesticides

sections.p: Patients present with marrow failure, organ infiltration and systemic symptoms.
b: Fatigue, pallor, easy bruising – anaemia & thrombocytopenia
Fever, neutropenia – infection risk
Bone pain, especially long bones – marrow expansion
Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly – extramedullary disease

sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, use a stepwise approach: start with smear, then marrow, then immunophenotype if available.
b: CBC with differential – looks for anemia, thrombocytopenia, blasts
Peripheral smear – quick clue of blasts
Bone‑marrow aspirate – definitive blast count
Flow cytometry – if available, confirms lineage

t.b: Is there anaemia, thrombocytopenia or leukocytosis? → Abnormal counts support marrow infiltration.
Are blasts seen? → Presence directs urgent referral; if absent, still consider marrow exam.
What is the blast percentage and morphology? → ≥20 % confirms ALL; also allows cytogenetics.
What lineage markers are present? → Use morphology and clinical picture to start provisional therapy; send sample to referral lab.

sections.p: Complications arise from tumour burden and treatment‑related toxicity.
b: Leukostasis (WBC > 100 × 10⁹/L) – respiratory or neurologic compromise
Tumour lysis syndrome – hyperuricaemia, renal failure
Severe neutropenic sepsis – fever with ANC < 0.5 × 10⁹/L
Intracranial haemorrhage – thrombocytopenia < 20 × 10⁹/L

sections.p: Therapy follows a risk‑adapted protocol: induction, consolidation, maintenance, plus supportive care.
b: Induction: steroids (prednisone), vincristine, L‑asparaginase, anthracycline – aims for remission
Supportive: prophylactic antibiotics, antifungals, tumour‑lysis prophylaxis (allopurinol or rasburicase if available), transfusion thresholds
Avoid: high‑dose cyclophosphamide in patients with hepatic dysfunction; avoid unnecessary NSAIDs when renal function is impaired

sections.p: Long‑term monitoring focuses on remission status, late effects and secondary malignancies.
b: MRD assessment after each phase – guides intensification
Annual cardiac echo if anthracyclines used
Vaccination updates after immune reconstitution
Counselling on fertility preservation where feasible

sections.p: Conditions that can mimic ALL clinically or on smear.
b: Acute myeloid leukaemia – myeloblasts, MPO⁺, CD33⁺
Severe aplastic anaemia – pancytopenia without blasts
Infectious mononucleosis – lymphocytosis, atypical lymphocytes

sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring or alarming.
b: Low peripheral blast count does not exclude marrow disease – always perform aspirate if suspicion remains
Hyperleukocytosis may be absent in T‑ALL despite high tumour burden
TdT negativity can occur in early T‑ALL; rely on full immunophenotype

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden respiratory distress or neurological change (leukostasis)

faq.q: Why is L‑asparaginase essential in ALL therapy?
faq.a: Leukaemic lymphoblasts cannot synthesize asparagine; the drug depletes plasma asparagine, starving the tumour while sparing normal cells.

faq.q: What does a high white‑cell count at presentation indicate?
faq.a: It is a poor prognostic factor, reflecting high tumour burden and increasing risk of leukostasis.

faq.q: Can ALL be cured in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Yes, with adapted protocols, early referral, supportive care and adherence to risk‑stratified chemotherapy.

exam: A 7‑year‑old presents with bone pain, bruising and a WBC of 70 × 10⁹/L. What is your immediate management and why? — Recognise leukostasis risk; start hydration, uric‑acid prophylaxis, and urgent induction while arranging transfer for intensive care.
How does flow cytometry differentiate ALL from AML, and why is this distinction critical? — CD19/CD10 (B‑ALL) or cCD3 (T‑ALL) vs MPO/CD33 (AML); guides chemotherapy regimen and prognosis.

A patient on induction develops rising creatinine and hyperuricaemia. What complication is likely and how do you treat it? — Tumour lysis syndrome; give aggressive IV fluids, allopurinol or rasburicase, and correct electrolytes.
Why would you avoid high‑dose cyclophosphamide in a patient with hepatitis B positivity? — Cyclophosphamide is hepatotoxic and can reactivate HBV, increasing liver failure risk.

What are the key cytogenetic abnormalities that move a patient into a high‑risk ALL group? — Philadelphia chromosome (t‑9;22), KMT2A (MLL) rearrangements, hypodiploidy; they mandate intensified therapy or targeted TKIs.

Explain how you would assess treatment response after induction in a setting without MRD testing. — Use repeat marrow morphology to confirm <5 % blasts; clinical remission (resolution of cytopenias) supports response.
A child with ALL develops a new scalp lesion. Which condition should you suspect and what is the next step? — Extramedullary disease (chloroma/leukaemia cutis); obtain biopsy and stage with imaging.
What red‑flag symptom in an ALL patient mandates immediate transfer to a higher‑level centre? — Acute respiratory distress or neurologic decline suggest leukostasis requiring ICU support.
